news_posts.post_content:
I came across a tool called Noisia today, and it made me rethink how I test PostgreSQL setups.

It is a workload generator built specifically to create harmful, chaotic conditions on a Postgres instance.

Think long-running transactions, deadlocks, idle transactions with locks held, and connection exhaustion, all on demand.

Most of us test happy paths.

We rarely simulate the messy stuff that actually takes production down at 2am.

A few things worth taking from this:

- Chaos testing your database is as valuable as chaos testing your services
- Idle-in-transaction connections are a silent killer that monitoring often misses
- Load testing without adversarial scenarios only tells half the story

The common mistake I see is teams load testing for throughput but never for pathological behavior.

A system that survives 10x traffic can still fall over from one badly behaved connection pool.

Have you ever deliberately broken your own database to see how it recovers?

news_posts.post_content:
Someone built a neural network entirely in SQL, and it is a genuinely interesting idea once you sit with it.

The core insight is simple.

A lot of array and tensor operations are secretly relational operations wearing a different costume.

Matrix multiplication, it turns out, can be expressed as a sum-product join followed by a group by.

Even gradient calculations for backpropagation map onto row-wise operations if you set the data model up right.

Why does this matter for us as data engineers.

- Query engines already solve distributed compute at massive scale
- Reframing ML workloads as relational ones could reuse decades of database optimization
- It blurs the line between the analytics engine and the ML platform

The part I find most compelling is the logical versus physical layer separation.

If a neural network is just a series of relations, your existing distributed SQL engine might already know how to scale it.

Do you think SQL engines will eventually absorb more of the ML workload, or will they stay separate stacks?

concept_posts.post_content:
Ever had a QuickSight dashboard that worked fine in dev but could not reach its data source in production.

VPC connectivity is usually the culprit.

QuickSight runs outside your VPC by default, which means it cannot see private resources like an RDS instance or an internal Redshift cluster.

To fix that, you create a VPC connection inside QuickSight that uses elastic network interfaces to reach into your private subnets.

A few things that trip people up:

- The security group attached to the ENI needs explicit inbound rules for QuickSight, not just your app servers
- Each VPC connection is tied to specific subnets, so multi-AZ setups need extra planning
- DNS resolution inside the VPC has to actually resolve your data source hostname, not just the IP

The common mistake is assuming a public data source and a VPC-connected one behave the same way during testing.

They do not, and that gap only shows up once you deploy for real users.

Have you run into VPC connectivity issues with your BI tools before?

concept_posts.post_content:
Batch ETL jobs running every few hours used to be good enough.

Now half the systems I work with expect near real-time data, and that is where Change Data Capture comes in.

CDC watches your source database's transaction log and streams every insert, update, and delete as it happens, instead of re-scanning entire tables on a schedule.

A few patterns worth knowing:

- Log-based CDC reads the database's write-ahead log directly, so it does not add query load to your source system
- Trigger-based CDC is easier to set up but can slow down writes on busy tables
- Downstream consumers need idempotent handling, since replays and retries are inevitable in any streaming setup

The common mistake is treating CDC as just a faster ETL.

It is really a different mental model, your pipeline now reacts to events instead of pulling snapshots.

That shift affects everything from schema evolution to how you think about data freshness.

Have you moved a pipeline from batch to CDC, and what broke first?
